Old Koskoosh, who had once been a great hunter and the chief of his tribe, sat by a small fire and listened greedily. <break time="0.8s" /> His eyes had grown dim long ago, but his hearing was still sharp, and every sound told him what was happening. <break time="0.8s" /> It was the sound of his own tribe breaking camp, for they were going on a long journey without him. <break time="0.8s" /> He heard Sit cum to ha, his sons daughter, shouting at the dogs and pushing them into their harnesses. <break time="0.8s" /> He heard his sons voice ordering the women to hurry, and the medicine man grunting as he loaded the last tent onto a sled. <break time="0.8s" /> Somewhere a child was crying, and Koskoosh thought that little Koo tee, who was weak and often sick, might not live long. <break time="0.8s" /> The tribe had to move quickly, because the winter day was short and the long trail would not wait. <break time="0.8s" /> Koskoosh did not blame them, for he knew that an old man who could not keep up would only slow the whole tribe down. <break time="0.8s" /> He had lived his life, and it was the young, not the old, who needed the food and the strength now.

At last his son. <break time="0.8s" /> The new chief of the tribe. <break time="0.8s" /> Came to him and asked. <break time="0.8s" /> Is it well with you. <break time="0.8s" /> It is well the old man answered. <break time="0.8s" /> And his son told him. <break time="0.8s" /> That there was wood beside him. <break time="0.8s" /> And that the fire burned bright. <break time="0.8s" /> The son said that the morning was gray. <break time="0.8s" /> And the cold had broken. <break time="0.8s" /> And that it would snow before long. <break time="0.8s" /> Yes, even now it is snowing. <break time="0.8s" /> Koskoosh agreed. <break time="0.8s" /> And the son explained. <break time="0.8s" /> That the tribe was hurrying. <break time="0.8s" /> Because their bundles were heavy. <break time="0.8s" /> He added that their stomachs were empty. <break time="0.8s" /> And the trail was long. <break time="0.8s" /> And then he asked once more. <break time="0.8s" /> If all was well. <break time="0.8s" /> It is well said Koskoosh. <break time="0.8s" /> For I am like last years leaf. <break time="0.8s" /> Hanging lightly on its stem. <break time="0.8s" /> And I will fall. <break time="0.8s" /> At the first breath of wind. <break time="0.8s" /> My eyes no longer show me the way. <break time="0.8s" /> My feet are heavy. <break time="0.8s" /> And I am tired. <break time="0.8s" /> He went on. <break time="0.8s" /> The son went away. <break time="0.8s" /> And Koskoosh listened. <break time="0.8s" /> Until the sound of his snowshoes faded. <break time="0.8s" /> And he knew. <break time="0.8s" /> That his son was gone forever. <break time="0.8s" /> It was then that he reached out. <break time="0.8s" /> And touched the small pile of wood. <break time="0.8s" /> That Sit cum to ha had gathered for him. <break time="0.8s" /> He thought that if she had cared more about her grandfather. <break time="0.8s" /> Than about the trail. <break time="0.8s" /> She would have gathered more.

마침내 그의 아들이. <break time="0.8s" /> 부족의 새 추장인. <break time="0.8s" /> 그에게 와서 물었다. <break time="0.8s" /> 괜찮으십니까. <break time="0.8s" /> 괜찮다 노인이 대답했다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그러자 아들이 그에게 말했다. <break time="0.8s" /> 곁에 장작이 있다고. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 불이 밝게 타고 있다고. <break time="0.8s" /> 아들은 말했다 아침이 잿빛이고. <break time="0.8s" /> 추위가 한풀 꺾였다고. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 머지않아 눈이 올 거라고. <break time="0.8s" /> 그래, 벌써 눈이 오는구나. <break time="0.8s" /> 코스쿠시가 맞장구쳤다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그러자 아들이 설명했다. <break time="0.8s" /> 부족이 서두르고 있다고. <break time="0.8s" /> 짐 꾸러미가 무겁기 때문에. <break time="0.8s" /> 그는 덧붙였다 그들의 배는 비어 있고. <break time="0.8s" /> 갈 길은 멀다고. <break time="0.8s" /> 그러고는 다시 한번 물었다. <break time="0.8s" /> 다 괜찮으시냐고. <break time="0.8s" /> 괜찮다 코스쿠시가 말했다. <break time="0.8s" /> 나는 작년의 나뭇잎 같으니까. <break time="0.8s" /> 줄기에 가볍게 매달린. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 나는 떨어질 거다. <break time="0.8s" /> 바람이 처음 한 번 불어오면. <break time="0.8s" /> 내 눈은 더 이상 길을 보여 주지 않고. <break time="0.8s" /> 발은 무겁고. <break time="0.8s" /> 나는 지쳤다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그가 말을 이었다. <break time="0.8s" /> 아들은 떠났다. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 코스쿠시는 귀를 기울였다. <break time="0.8s" /> 설피 소리가 희미해질 때까지. <break time="0.8s" /> 그래서 그는 알게 되었다. <break time="0.8s" /> 아들이 영영 가 버렸다는 것을. <break time="0.8s" /> 바로 그때였다 그가 손을 뻗은 것은. <break time="0.8s" /> 그리고 작은 장작 더미를 만졌다. <break time="0.8s" /> 싯쿰토하가 그를 위해 모아 둔. <break time="0.8s" /> 그는 생각했다 그 아이가 할아버지를 더 생각했더라면. <break time="0.8s" /> 갈 길보다. <break time="0.8s" /> 장작을 더 모아 두었을 거라고.

For a moment he wondered whether his son would soften. <break time="0.8s" /> And come back with the dogs. <break time="0.8s" /> To take him along. <break time="0.8s" /> But he soon let the thought go. <break time="0.8s" /> Because he knew. <break time="0.8s" /> That this was the law. <break time="0.8s" /> Of all living things. <break time="0.8s" /> Nature did not care about a single life. <break time="0.8s" /> And the only task. <break time="0.8s" /> That she gave to every creature. <break time="0.8s" /> Was to have young ones. <break time="0.8s" /> When that task was done. <break time="0.8s" /> Death came. <break time="0.8s" /> And this was the rule. <break time="0.8s" /> That every creature had to obey. <break time="0.8s" /> In the end. <break time="0.8s" /> The mosquito vanished. <break time="0.8s" /> With the first frost. <break time="0.8s" /> And the little tree squirrel crept away. <break time="0.8s" /> To die alone. <break time="0.8s" /> The old rabbit grew too slow. <break time="0.8s" /> To run from its enemies. <break time="0.8s" /> And even the great bear. <break time="0.8s" /> Became blind and clumsy at last. <break time="0.8s" /> In his strong years. <break time="0.8s" /> He had led his people as their chief. <break time="0.8s" /> And he too had once made a hard choice. <break time="0.8s" /> Like his sons. <break time="0.8s" /> Long ago one winter before the missionary came. <break time="0.8s" /> He had left his own father behind. <break time="0.8s" /> On an upper reach of the Klondike. <break time="0.8s" /> It was not cruelty. <break time="0.8s" /> That made him do it. <break time="0.8s" /> But the same law. <break time="0.8s" /> That now left him alone by the fire.

For a moment he wondered whether his son would soften and come back with the dogs to take him along. <break time="0.8s" /> But he soon let the thought go, because he knew that this was the law of all living things. <break time="0.8s" /> Nature did not care about a single life, and the only task that she gave to every creature was to have young ones. <break time="0.8s" /> When that task was done, death came, and this was the rule that every creature had to obey in the end. <break time="0.8s" /> The mosquito vanished with the first frost, and the little tree squirrel crept away to die alone. <break time="0.8s" /> The old rabbit grew too slow to run from its enemies, and even the great bear became blind and clumsy at last. <break time="0.8s" /> In his strong years he had led his people as their chief, and he too had once made a hard choice like his sons. <break time="0.8s" /> Long ago, one winter before the missionary came, he had left his own father behind on an upper reach of the Klondike. <break time="0.8s" /> It was not cruelty that made him do it, but the same law that now left him alone by the fire.
